title: Danielle Smith warns of party fracture in speech to UCP received by cheers and boos

image.caption: United Conservative Party Leader Danielle Smith addresses party members at their annual meeting in Calgary on Nov. 28. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Calgary·New

In a speech delivered on the convention floor to a divided audience, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith reiterated calls for her party to unite lest it "fracture" and lose the next election to what she characterized as the "radical" Opposition NDP.
Premier's speech to her party comes with next election less than a year away

In a speech delivered on the convention floor Saturday, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith reiterated calls for her party to unite lest it "fracture" and lose the next election to what she characterized as the "radical" Opposition NDP.

Alberta's United Conservatives are meeting this weekend at Calgary's BMO Centre for their annual general meeting, the fifth held under Smith. But this year's gathering has seen some attendees divided into warring camps — those promoting unity in the party, and those who want it to go another way.
"We must be unified. If we aren’t, our party will lose government — and Albertans will suffer terribly," Smith told the crowd.
At least today, the goal of unity seemed an elusive one amongst some in the crowd. Smith's speech was marked by scattered boos and the odd shout of "freedom!"
Some attendees sitting at the back of the room held up yellow cards that read: "I voted for Option #2," referring to the separation option on the ballot in the recent Alberta referendum.
Attendees at the 2026 United Conservative Party annual general meeting hold up yellow cards that read, 'I voted for Option #2.' (Jason Markusoff/CBC)
But Smith's speech also drew cheers, including in segments where the premier pointed to her government's work on energy and economic matters, such as when it came to the Pacific Link pipeline.
Independence leaders have said that hard feelings remain amongst those who championed Option 2 in the referendum, especially given certain moves the party has taken of late.

blocks.text: On the convention floor, the most notable of those moves concerns the party requiring constituency board presidents to publicly respect and abide by the result delivered by the referendum.
Smith reiterated the party's position on that front in her speech, while promising the party would not subject its members to "ideological purity tests."

United Conservative Party leader Danielle Smith, right, greets her mother Sharon Smith before addressing party members at their annual meeting in Calgary on Nov. 28. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)
Board election votes to come
There was a long lineup at the BMO Centre on Saturday morning, with attendees waiting their turn to vote for new members to sit on the provincial board. Eight spots are up for grabs this year.
These individuals set the rules and the processes for nomination and platform development.

On Friday, Colin Aitchison, a former spokesperson for the UCP under ministers Adriana LaGrange and Nicholas Milliken, told CBC News he expected a strong mandate on the "unity" front in those elections, while well-known separatist leader Mitch Sylvestre said he hoped for a strong result for his side.
Attendees line up to vote for the board of the United Conservative Party on Saturday morning. (Joel Dryden/CBC)
Joseph Poirier was one of those people waiting in line to vote. He said a friend of his invited him to the event.
"Everyone's engaged and interested in this event. It's going to be a big one," he said. "A lot of people are feeling uncomfortable with the direction Smith is taking.
"She's done a lot of good things, but she's upset her base a lot too."
This year's attendee count has swelled to more than 8,000, which the party says is a record.
Rick Boucher, an attendee from Fort McMurray-Lac La Biche, said he joined the party in September of this year.
He gave a positive review to Smith's speech, adding he felt the premier had a difficult job in trying to secure party unity.

"I'm pleased to see that, through her efforts, there is now a good relationship, in my opinion, with the federal government," Boucher said. "That's what we need to do. Work together for the benefit of all people of this province, and of this country."
Board election results are expected on Saturday evening. Members will also vote Saturday on a series of grassroots policy resolutions.
